title: Applied anatomy: the cubital fossa, antecubital veins and supracondylar fracture

guidelineVersions: BOAST Supracondylar Fractures of the Humerus in Children (v2, Oct 2020)
Babal et al., J Pediatr Orthop (2010)

related.why: Same method for the upper limb: map the deficit onto the nerve

brief.role: Core surgical trainee in the emergency department
brief.scenario: Lily Fenwick, 6, fell from a climbing frame onto her outstretched left hand. Her elbow is swollen and deformed and she will not move it. The examiner will ask you about the anatomy of the cubital fossa and read out her radiograph findings.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on the cubital fossa and its veins, and on the structures at risk from her injury.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Borders, contents medial to lateral, veins in the roof. Then the fracture: which way the fragment went decides what is hurt.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Checking the median nerve with sensation only. The anterior interosseous nerve has no skin territory.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Pronator teres medially, brachioradialis laterally, the epicondylar line above."

grid.label: Borders, roof and floor
grid.fail: Names brachialis as a border, or cannot give the medial and lateral borders.
grid.pass: Line between the epicondyles above, pronator teres medially, brachioradialis laterally. Floor brachialis and supinator. Roof includes bicipital aponeurosis.
grid.high: Adds that the apex is where brachioradialis meets pronator teres, and that the median cubital vein lies in the roof.

grid.label: Contents and venepuncture
grid.fail: Cannot give the contents in order, or would needle the medial side blind.
grid.pass: Medial to lateral: median nerve, brachial artery, biceps tendon, radial nerve. Median cubital vein preferred for venepuncture.
grid.high: Explains the bicipital aponeurosis lies between the median cubital vein and the brachial artery and median nerve; medially the artery is at risk.

grid.label: Displacement and structures at risk
grid.fail: Names the median nerve only, with no link to direction of displacement.
grid.pass: Extension type: distal fragment posterior. Posterolateral displacement endangers median nerve and brachial artery; posteromedial displacement endangers the radial nerve.
grid.high: Anterior interosseous nerve injury predominates in extension-type fractures; a medial wire endangers the ulnar nerve.

grid.label: Nerve examination
grid.fail: Tests sensation only, or omits the anterior interosseous nerve.
grid.pass: Tests and documents each nerve: OK sign for anterior interosseous, thumb abduction and sensation for median, wrist extension for radial, finger abduction for ulnar.
grid.high: States the anterior interosseous nerve is purely motor, so a sensory check alone misses it; documents before and after reduction.

grid.label: Vascular status
grid.fail: Does not check the radial pulse and perfusion, or plans routine brachial exploration.
grid.pass: Documents radial pulse and hand perfusion; absent pulse or poor perfusion needs urgent reduction on the day.
grid.high: Pink pulseless hand usually recovers after reduction; a hand still ischaemic after reduction needs brachial artery exploration.

grid.label: Compartment syndrome
grid.fail: Relies on pulses or the five Ps to exclude compartment syndrome.
grid.pass: Watches the forearm flexor compartment: pain on passive finger extension, tense forearm, escalating pain; urgent senior review.
grid.high: In children, a rising analgesia requirement is an early warning sign; a lost pulse is late.

grid.label: Surgical stabilisation
grid.fail: Would treat a displaced fracture in a cast alone.
grid.pass: Displaced fracture: reduction and K-wire fixation, on the day of injury.
grid.high: At least two 2 mm wires engaging the cortex proximal to the fracture; if a medial wire is used, protect and record the ulnar nerve.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Epicondylar line, pronator teres and brachioradialis, meeting at the apex. The median cubital vein runs in the roof.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Why is the median cubital vein the safe choice?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The bicipital aponeurosis lies between it and the brachial artery and median nerve. Medially that protection thins, so the artery is at risk.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Which nerve is injured most often?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: In extension-type fractures, the anterior interosseous nerve. A medial wire puts the ulnar nerve at risk.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The anterior interosseous nerve is purely motor, so a sensory check alone misses it. I'd document before and after reduction.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: After reduction her hand is pink but pulseless.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Most perfusion problems recover with reduction, so I'd monitor closely. If the hand stays ischaemic, the brachial artery needs exploring.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: In a child, a rising analgesia requirement is an early warning. Losing the pulse is late.

high.speaker: candidate

failures.consequence: Misses an anterior interosseous nerve palsy, which has no sensory loss.

failures.move: Not documenting the radial pulse and perfusion.
failures.consequence: A vascular injury is missed, or a later change cannot be recognised.

failures.move: Using a present pulse to exclude compartment syndrome.
failures.consequence: Delayed fasciotomy and Volkmann's ischaemic contracture.
Risks puncturing the brachial artery or injuring the median nerve.

recovery.line: Medial to lateral: median nerve, brachial artery, biceps tendon, radial nerve.

recovery.when: Asked which nerve is at risk
recovery.line: It depends on where the distal fragment went: posterolateral puts the median nerve and artery at risk, posteromedial the radial.

knowledge.fact: Borders: epicondylar line, pronator teres, brachioradialis. Floor brachialis and supinator.
Contents medial to lateral: median nerve, brachial artery, biceps tendon, radial nerve.
Anterior interosseous nerve injury predominates in extension-type fractures; medial pins endanger the ulnar nerve.
Document neurovascular status at presentation and before surgery; operate on the day of injury.
Explore the brachial artery if the hand stays ischaemic after reduction.
Rising analgesia requirement is an early sign of compartment syndrome in children.

recall.think: Displaced supracondylar fracture: nerve, brachial artery, compartment syndrome.
recall.say: "Posterolateral displacement: median nerve and brachial artery at risk."
do: Document pulse, perfusion and each nerve
OK sign for anterior interosseous nerve

numbers.meaning: of nerve injuries in extension-type fractures are anterior interosseous

recall.trap: A normal sensory check does not clear the anterior interosseous nerve.
recall.finish: Reduction and K-wire fixation; explore the artery if still ischaemic after reduction.

partner.opening: Lily has injured her left elbow. Tell me the borders of the cubital fossa.

reveals.finding: Read out: AP and lateral radiographs of the left elbow show a fracture line running across the distal humerus just above the epicondyles. The fragments have no cortical contact. On the lateral view the distal fragment and forearm lie behind the humeral shaft; on the AP view the distal fragment is shifted laterally.

reveals.trigger: Candidate tests the anterior interosseous nerve
reveals.finding: Cannot make an OK sign; sensation in the hand normal.
Radial pulse not palpable; hand warm and pink; capillary refill 2 seconds.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about the evening after surgery
reveals.finding: She needed three extra doses of analgesia and cries when her fingers are straightened.

push.question: What are the borders of the cubital fossa?
Which vein would you use and why?
push.expect: Median cubital; bicipital aponeurosis protects artery and nerve.

push.question: In a prosection of the left cubital fossa, a large tendon runs down the middle of the fossa to the forearm. What lies immediately medial to it, what lies medial to that, and what lies on its lateral side?
push.expect: Brachial artery immediately medial to the biceps tendon, then the median nerve; the radial nerve lies laterally, under brachioradialis.

push.question: A superficial vein crosses the front of the elbow obliquely, running upwards and medially to join the vein on the lateral side of the forearm to the vein on the medial side. A flat sheet of fascia separates it from the deeper structures. Name the three veins and the fascial sheet, and explain why this vein is the preferred venepuncture site.
push.expect: Median cubital vein joining the cephalic (lateral) to the basilic (medial) vein; the bicipital aponeurosis lies between it and the brachial artery and median nerve.

push.question: What is at risk with posterolateral displacement?
How would you test the anterior interosseous nerve?
push.expect: OK sign: flexor pollicis longus and index profundus.

push.question: Her hand is pink but pulseless after reduction. Explore?
How would you fix it?
push.expect: At least two 2 mm K-wires; protect ulnar nerve if medial wire.

curveballs.prompt: She can't make an OK sign but her sensation is normal.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Anterior interosseous nerve palsy: purely motor. Document it before reduction.

curveballs.prompt: After a medial wire, her little finger is numb.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Possible iatrogenic ulnar nerve injury: document, inform the senior surgeon, consider removing or re-siting the medial wire.

curveballs.prompt: Her pulse is present but she needs more and more morphine.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Treat as compartment syndrome until proven otherwise: split dressings, urgent senior review, fasciotomy if confirmed.
